strapline: The treason bail plea clears its first hurdle; 1,558 Copperbelt teachers ordered to rural schools; Canada returns to Lusaka; and Daka out of Burundi

stories.title: 'Properly before the court': the High Court rejects the State's objection and clears the way for the 18 treason accused to argue for bail, as the sedition bail plea slips to Monday
stories.excerpt: A three-judge panel of the Lusaka High Court ruled on Tuesday 10 November that the constitutional bail application by Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 co-accused was properly before it, rejecting the State's argument that it had been started in the wrong registry. Nobody has been released: the ruling only means the application will now be heard. A day earlier, the pair's other bail plea, in the sedition case, was adjourned again after the State said it had a preliminary issue to raise.

image.label: Day 74 at the High Court
image.caption: The ruling removes a procedural objection, not the accused from custody: the question of whether 18 people held since August should be freed is still to be argued.

body: The constitutional bail application that has been adjourned, re-listed and argued over since October can now be heard. The Lusaka High Court ruled on Tuesday 10 November that the application by the defeated presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, his running mate Makebi Zulu and 16 other people charged with treason is properly before the court, Zambia Monitor reported on Wednesday morning. The Maravi Post, carrying a Muvi TV report, described the decision the same way: a procedural hurdle has been cleared and the substantive arguments on release can proceed.

The State had raised a preliminary objection, arguing that the application had been wrongly commenced as a civil petition rather than through the criminal registry and should be dismissed for want of jurisdiction, Zambia Monitor reported. The defence answered that the objection did not touch the central question, which is whether keeping the 18 in custody without trial is constitutional; their case rests on Articles 13 and 28 of the Constitution and asks for unconditional release or bail on reasonable conditions. The application names the Attorney General, Mulilo Kabesha, and the Director of Public Prosecutions, Gilbert Phiri, as respondents.

The panel hearing the treason matter is made up of Justices Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga, according to Zambia Monitor; The Zambian Observer listed the same three judges in its account of Tuesday's sitting, which it said resumed at midday under heavy security that at times kept relatives and journalists away from the building.

body.text: We continue praying for openness, fairness and justice to prevail
body.attribution: Brian Mundubile, in a statement after the ruling, as quoted by Zambia Monitor on Wednesday 11 November

body.text: What the ruling does not do

body: Both reports are careful on this point. The court has not ordered anyone's release and has not yet heard the bail arguments themselves; the Maravi Post's report says plainly that the development should not be mistaken for a bail victory. The 18 remain at Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison in Kabwe, where they have been held since August on allegations of treason and of sedition and terrorism-related offences, all of which they deny. Zambia Monitor said Mr Zulu, a constitutional lawyer, has been granted leave to represent himself. Neither report gives a date for the substantive hearing.

The defence's argument, set out by Sakwiba Sikota SC before Tuesday's sitting and reported by The Zambian Observer, is that the accused have been held far beyond the 48 hours within which a detained person should be brought before a court, that prosecutors still describe their investigation as continuing, and that some of the co-accused have arrived in court hungry because of delays in transporting them from Kabwe. The Observer, which put Tuesday at day 74 since the arrests, said Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu had spent Monday night in custody in Lusaka rather than making the roughly 150-kilometre return trip to Mukobeko.

body.text: The sedition bail plea waits for a Monday

body: The two men also face a separate case: two counts of seditious practices under section 57 of the Penal Code over Facebook livestreams on 14 August 2026, the day after the general election, in which prosecutors say they claimed that their parallel vote tabulation showed the NRPUP had won and demanded that the Electoral Commission of Zambia publish the results. That case was transferred from Solwezi to the Lusaka High Court by Judge Edward Musona on 5 November, the Times of Zambia reported.

Their bail application in that case was due to be heard on Monday 9 November but did not proceed. The State asked for an adjournment so that it could raise a preliminary issue, without saying what it was, and the court granted the request and adjourned the hearing to the following Monday, the Times of Zambia and News Diggers reported. The Zambian Observer, carrying a Phoenix FM report, said the panel, led by Judge Geoffrey Mulenga and sitting in chambers, gave the State until the next day to file its preliminary application. Mr Sikota complained that the State raises a preliminary issue every time the matter comes up, and said the bail application had been filed on 19 October and had still not been heard.

body.title: Two cases, two panels
items: **Treason** — 18 accused including Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and the former Anglican bishop Trevor Mwamba; constitutional bail application ruled properly before the court on Tuesday 10 November; panel Justices Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga.
**Sedition** — Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu only; two counts under section 57; bail hearing adjourned on Monday 9 November to the following Monday; panel led by Judge Geoffrey Mulenga.
**Custody** — all 18 remain at Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison in Kabwe.

body.confirmed: The High Court ruled on Tuesday 10 November that the constitutional bail application by the 18 treason accused is properly before it (Zambia Monitor; Maravi Post citing Muvi TV). No release has been ordered. The sedition bail hearing was adjourned on Monday 9 November to the following Monday after the State sought time to raise a preliminary issue (Times of Zambia; News Diggers; The Zambian Observer citing Phoenix FM).
body.unverified: The date of the substantive constitutional bail hearing has not been reported. Outlets differ on when the 18 were taken into custody: Zambia Monitor says 14 August, The Zambian Observer says 27 August. One Zambian Observer report said the sedition matter had been set down for ruling on Friday 13 November rather than Monday; the Times of Zambia, News Diggers and the Observer's own Phoenix FM report all say Monday. The content of the State's preliminary issue in the sedition case has not been disclosed.

stories.title: 1,247 in Kitwe and 311 in Ndola: the Copperbelt minister orders 1,558 'excess' teachers out to rural schools, as Musokotwane says there will be no teacher recruitment in 2027
stories.excerpt: Emmanuel Kasambo says urban schools on the Copperbelt are carrying 1,558 more teachers than their establishments allow while rural classrooms go without, and has given provincial officials a week to complete the staffing count that will move them. On ZNBC's Sunday Interview the Finance Minister said the government would recruit no teachers next year until it knows where the real gaps are.

image.label: 1,558 transfers
image.caption: Two ministers, one diagnosis: teachers posted to rural schools drift back to town, and the government says it will not hire more until it has counted who is actually where.

body: The Copperbelt Province Minister, Emmanuel Kasambo, has ordered 1,558 teachers in Kitwe and Ndola to be moved to rural schools, saying they are surplus to the establishments of the urban schools where they draw their salaries while schools in outlying districts go short, The Zambian Observer reported on Tuesday 10 November. Speaking in Ndola after meeting representatives of teachers' unions, he gave the breakdown as 1,247 excess teachers in Kitwe, 699 of them in primary schools and 548 in secondary schools, and 311 in Ndola, 159 primary and 152 secondary, a figure he said would be revisited.

News Diggers reported on Monday that Mr Kasambo had first issued the directive at the Nsengele Kununka traditional ceremony of the Bulima people in Mpongwe District on Sunday 8 November, where he told the Provincial Permanent Secretary, the Provincial Education Officer and the District Education Board Secretaries that they had one week to complete a staffing assessment and provide the information needed for the exercise. Teachers who refuse a lawful transfer face disciplinary action, that report said; the Observer's account of his Ndola remarks was blunter, quoting him as saying that those who refuse rural postings will be dismissed.

Mr Kasambo also warned education board secretaries against facilitating transfers from rural to urban schools, saying some teachers arrive in town with letters from Lusaka after only a few months in a rural district, in breach of a Cabinet decision that requires four years of service before a transfer is considered. Officials who arrange such moves would face action, he said, according to The Zambian Observer.

The provincial order lands in the same week as a national one. The Finance and National Planning Minister, Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane, told ZNBC's Sunday Interview that the government has no plans to recruit teachers in 2027, News Diggers, The Zambian Observer and the Times of Zambia all reported. His reason was the same as Mr Kasambo's: the government cannot know the true shortage until teachers are where their records say they are.

body.text: No, for next year there is no plan to recruit teachers.
body.attribution: Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane, Minister of Finance and National Planning, on ZNBC's Sunday Interview, as quoted by News Diggers on Tuesday 10 November

body: Dr Musokotwane gave examples, as reported by the Times of Zambia: schools with an establishment of five or six teachers where only two or three report for duty, and schools with an establishment of six or seven that have 20 or 25. He called it a longstanding administrative problem, said teachers should return to their designated stations so that genuine gaps can be identified, and said deployment is one of the functions that ought to be decentralised to district level, The Zambian Observer reported.

None of Tuesday's reports carried a response from the teachers' unions to the Copperbelt directive or to the recruitment freeze, and neither minister said how long the counting exercise would take nationally or what would happen to teachers found to be at the wrong school outside the Copperbelt.

body.title: The Copperbelt numbers, as given by Mr Kasambo
items: **Kitwe** — 1,247 excess teachers: 699 primary, 548 secondary.
**Ndola** — 311 excess teachers: 159 primary, 152 secondary; to be revisited.
**Deadline** — one week for provincial and district officials to complete a staffing assessment (News Diggers, 9 November).
**Transfer rule** — four years' service before a transfer is considered, under a Cabinet decision he cited.

stories.title: Back after 15 years: Canada reopens its High Commission in Lusaka with US$10.5 million in new support and a cooperation agreement that names critical minerals first
stories.excerpt: Canada's Secretary of State for International Development, Randeep Sarai, opened the mission on Monday 9 November alongside Mulambo Haimbe and Situmbeko Musokotwane, announcing US$10.5 million for growth, women's empowerment, energy access and institutions. Zambia had been handled from Dar es Salaam for more than a decade; Corry Van Gaal is the new High Commissioner.

image.label: Ottawa returns to Lusaka
image.caption: A mission closed for about 15 years reopens with a development package and an agreement covering trade, critical minerals and regional security.

body: Canada formally reopened its High Commission in Lusaka on Monday 9 November, ending a period of roughly 15 years in which its relations with Zambia were run from its mission in Dar es Salaam, Zambia Monitor, the Voice of Nigeria and The Zambian Observer reported. The opening was performed by Randeep Sarai, Canada's Secretary of State for International Development, with the Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister, Mulambo Haimbe, and the Finance and National Planning Minister, Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane, among the Zambian officials present, Zambia Monitor reported.

Mr Sarai used the occasion to announce US$10.5 million in new Canadian support for Zambia, aimed at economic growth, women's empowerment, energy access and the strengthening of institutions, according to Zambia Monitor. The two governments also signed an Agreement on Economic and Development Cooperation covering trade and investment, critical minerals, private-sector development, regional security and inclusive growth.

body.text: The opening of Canada's High Commission in Lusaka marks a new chapter in the relationship between our two countries
body.attribution: Randeep Sarai, Canada's Secretary of State for International Development, at the opening in Lusaka on Monday 9 November, as quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: The scale of Canadian interest in Zambia is mostly in the mines. The Voice of Nigeria, carrying an APA report, put Canadian mining assets in Zambia at about US$12 billion in 2024, enough to make Zambia the fifth-largest destination for Canadian mining investment abroad; Mr Haimbe, as reported by The Zambian Observer from a Muvi TV report, gave a figure of more than US$12.9 billion. Both reports put bilateral trade at US$97 million in 2025, a modest figure that the Zambian side says it wants to double within five years. The sectors named for new activity were mining, renewable energy, fibre processing and small business.

Mr Sarai said Canada had provided more than US$210 million in international assistance to Zambia since 2020, Zambia Monitor reported; the APA report gives the same sum but dates it from 2021. Zambia Monitor also recalled the Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's recent announcement of a planned US$50 million loan from FinDev Canada to Zanaco, intended for women-owned businesses, agribusinesses and small and medium-sized enterprises, and noted the two countries' long joint work on ending child, early and forced marriage, including co-sponsoring the first UN General Assembly resolution on the subject in 2013.

The new High Commissioner, Corry Van Gaal, has more than 20 years in international affairs, including senior posts at Global Affairs Canada, work with the World Bank's Global Agriculture and Food Security Program and postings across Africa and South America, The Zambian Observer reported. She described the reopening as a chance to deepen economic collaboration and open new areas of partnership, according to the APA report, while Mr Haimbe said a resident Canadian mission would strengthen economic relations and support Zambia's efforts to attract investment.

body.title: Canada and Zambia, by the numbers
items: **US$10.5 million** — new support announced on Monday (Zambia Monitor).
**US$210 million** — Canadian assistance since 2020 (Mr Sarai) or 2021 (APA).
**US$12 billion to US$12.9 billion** — Canadian mining assets in Zambia, depending on the report.
**US$97 million** — bilateral trade in 2025, which Lusaka wants to double in five years.
**US$50 million** — planned FinDev Canada loan to Zanaco announced by Prime Minister Carney.

stories.title: 'Business should not be done through the courts': Hichilema and Trafigura's chairman agree a reset, with legal disputes to settle and concentrate exports in the President's sights
stories.excerpt: President Hichilema received a delegation led by Trafigura's chairman Jeremy Weir at State House on Monday 9 November and said afterwards that the two sides had agreed to reset their relationship. News Diggers reports that he asked for outstanding legal disputes to be resolved and for Zambia to stop exporting mineral concentrates. His former policy adviser Chipokota Mwanawasa was recently appointed the trader's Country Executive Director for Zambia.

image.label: State House, 9 November
image.caption: A commodity trader with copper, fuel and logistics interests in Zambia is invited to help with three Grow Zambia targets, starting with three million tonnes of copper by 2031.

body: President Hakainde Hichilema met a delegation from the commodity trader Trafigura, led by its chairman Jeremy Weir, at State House on Monday 9 November, and said afterwards that the government and the company had agreed to reset their relationship, Open Zambia, The Zambian Observer and News Diggers reported. In a statement addressed to citizens after the meeting, reported by Open Zambia and the Observer, the President thanked Trafigura for its long-standing interest in Zambia and for the jobs it supports, including through Puma Energy and Servara, and said the aim was a partnership that delivers for Zambians.

News Diggers reported two further points from the meeting. The President called for the outstanding legal disputes between the government and Trafigura to be resolved, saying business should not be conducted through the courts, and he said Zambia should stop exporting mineral concentrates and invest instead in refining capacity. Neither the Open Zambia nor the Observer account mentions the disputes or the concentrates, and none of the three reports describes what the disputes are about.

body.text: We look forward to a partnership that delivers more investment, more jobs and more opportunity for Zambian businesses
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, in a statement after meeting the Trafigura delegation at State House on Monday 9 November, as quoted by Open Zambia and The Zambian Observer

body: Trafigura buys and finances copper, moves fuel and builds the logistics that connect producers to markets, and the President's statement mapped those three strengths onto three Grow Zambia Agenda goals: three million tonnes of copper a year by 2031, reliable and affordable energy, and links to regional and global markets, Open Zambia reported. He suggested the company could play a direct part in all three.

The meeting follows Trafigura's recent appointment of Chipokota Mwanawasa, until recently Policy Adviser to the President, as its Country Executive Director for Zambia, a move News Diggers noted in its report, which describes the company as a multinational that sources, stores, blends and transports raw materials and energy products.

What the reset means in practice has not been spelt out. No agreement, investment figure or timetable was announced in any of the three reports, and Trafigura's own account of the meeting was not reported. The two concrete tests will be whether the disputes the President referred to are settled and whether the company's copper business in Zambia moves towards refined metal rather than concentrate, as he asked.

stories.title: 16,000 megawatts on paper, 4,722 on the grid: Kapala visits the ERB and calls in the developers whose signed power deals cannot find the money to build
stories.excerpt: The new Minister of Electricity, Peter Kapala, used a familiarisation visit to the Energy Regulation Board on Monday 9 November to ask why projects with signed power purchase agreements are not reaching financial close. The ERB's chairman put the signed pipeline at more than 16,000 MW; the national target is 10,000 MW of capacity by 2031, from 4,722 MW in October.

image.label: Signed but not financed
image.caption: The regulator says the problem is not a shortage of projects but a shortage of closed financing; the minister wants a meeting with the developers to find out why.

body: Zambia has more than 16,000 megawatts of proposed generation capacity sitting in signed power purchase agreements, and the main reason most of it is not being built is that the developers cannot get their financing closed. That was the message the Energy Regulation Board's chairman, James Banda, gave the Minister of Electricity, Peter Kapala, during the minister's familiarisation visit to the regulator on Monday 9 November, The Zambian Observer reported on Tuesday 10 November and the Ecofin Agency reported on Wednesday.

Mr Kapala said he would convene a meeting with renewable-energy developers to identify solutions, and listed his priorities as getting signed agreements to financial close, finalising the framework for an Independent System Operator, speeding up electric-vehicle charging infrastructure and expanding transmission, the Observer reported. He said the government wants to turn investor interest into working plants and reach 10,000 MW of generation capacity by 2031, and expressed the hope that the Zambia–Tanzania interconnector would be completed in time to meet demand, particularly from the mines.

body.text: The gap between the pipeline and the plug

body: Installed capacity rose from 3,777 MW in 2024 to 4,722 MW in October 2026, according to Ministry of Energy figures cited by Ecofin, which means the 2031 target needs more than 5,000 MW of new capacity in five years. Mr Banda told the Observer that some developers were being asked by financiers for requirements already covered by the Ministry of Energy's investment framework, and urged sponsors to comply with the framework before submitting agreements for regulatory approval; he proposed closer coordination between the ministry, the ERB and project sponsors.

Ecofin set out the wider obstacles identified by others: doubts about whether ZESCO and other buyers can pay independent producers, exchange-rate movements and transmission constraints flagged by the International Energy Agency, and a 2025 World Bank analysis that said Zambia's fiscal position limited the sovereign guarantees it could offer private power projects. The government's responses, the agency reported, include a coordinated procurement framework approved in December 2025, new procurement, incentive and financing guidelines published in May 2026, and a renewable-energy liquidity mechanism, backed by the UK-funded Green Cities, Infrastructure and Energy Programme, to cushion projects against short-term payment problems.

The ERB's Director General, Elijah Sichone, told the minister that net metering, under which customers with their own solar panels feed power into the grid, had reached about 32 MW against a target of 100 MW, and called for a collective push to accelerate it, the Observer reported. Mr Banda said the Board supported the government's decision to create a dedicated Ministry of Electricity.

body.title: The numbers from the ERB visit
items: **16,000 MW+** — proposed capacity in projects with signed PPAs (James Banda, ERB).
**4,722 MW** — installed capacity in October 2026, up from 3,777 MW in 2024 (Ministry of Energy, via Ecofin).
**10,000 MW** — government target for 2031.
**32 MW of 100 MW** — net metering achieved against target (Elijah Sichone, ERB).

stories.title: A plea agreement, not yet filed: the State says it has a deal with David Kazadi and two co-accused in the obscene-material case, and the magistrate gives it until close of business
stories.excerpt: The trial of the film producer David Kazadi, the social-media figure Mwaka Halwindi and Ruby Muzandu on eight counts of producing, possessing and circulating obscene material was due to start on Tuesday 10 November. Instead the prosecution told the Lusaka Magistrates' Court it had reached an agreement under the Plea Negotiations and Agreements Act. Its terms have not been disclosed; the case returns on 18 November.

image.label: Act No. 20 of 2010
image.caption: A 2010 law that prosecutors and the Judiciary have been trying to revive is invoked in a case that had been heading for trial.

body: The State has reached a plea-negotiation agreement with the three people accused in Lusaka's obscene-material case, and has asked for time to serve it on the defence and file it with the court, Zambia Monitor and News Diggers reported on Tuesday 10 November. The accused are the film producer David Kazadi, the social-media personality Mwaka Halwindi and Ruby Muzandu, who between them face eight counts of producing, possessing and circulating obscene material covering the period from 1 January 2023 to 30 June 2025, News Diggers reported.

All three had pleaded not guilty: Mr Kazadi and Ms Halwindi to every count, and Ms Muzandu to the counts of possessing and circulating the material, according to News Diggers. The agreement is being made under the Plea Negotiations and Agreements Act No. 20 of 2010, Zambia Monitor reported.

When the matter came before Magistrate Kawama Mwamfuli at the Lusaka Magistrates' Court on Tuesday, the agreement had not yet been served on the defence or filed, Zambia Monitor reported. The magistrate ordered the State, represented by Senior Public Prosecutor Judith Mauka and Public Prosecutor Hope Mikwala, to serve and file it by close of business, and adjourned the case to Wednesday 18 November for the prosecution's application. A trial sitting in September had been put off because the magistrate was hearing election petition tribunal matters.

Neither report sets out what the agreement contains: whether any of the three would plead guilty to any count, to what, or what sentence the State would propose. The 18 November hearing, when the prosecution makes its application, will be the first public test of the deal. Zambia Monitor noted that the National Prosecution Authority, the Law Association of Zambia, the Legal Aid Board and the Judiciary have all been promoting plea bargaining, a procedure that has been little used since the Act came into force.

body.confirmed: The State told the Lusaka Magistrates' Court on Tuesday 10 November that it had reached a plea-negotiation agreement with the three accused; the court ordered it served and filed by close of business and adjourned the case to 18 November (Zambia Monitor; News Diggers). The accused had pleaded not guilty (News Diggers).
body.unverified: The terms of the agreement, including which counts, if any, would be admitted and what sentence the State would propose, have not been reported. The charges remain allegations, and no plea under the agreement has yet been entered or accepted by the court.

stories.title: Daka, Lameck Banda and Gamphani Lungu are out of both Burundi games: three injuries, three replacements, and three Europe-based arrivals land in Ndola on the same afternoon
stories.excerpt: Patson Daka's ankle, hurt in Hamburg's win over Mönchengladbach on 6 November, has cost Zambia its first-choice striker for Friday's qualifier at Levy Mwanawasa and the return in Bujumbura. Team doctor George Magwende says all three recoveries exceed seven days. Edward Chilufya, Derrick Bulaya and Prince Mumba come in; Chanka Zimba, Joseph Liteta and David Hamansenya flew in on Tuesday.

image.label: Three out, three in
image.caption: Zambia go into the Burundi double-header second in Group I, a point behind Algeria, without the Hamburg striker who had only just returned from a thigh injury.

body: Patson Daka, Lameck Banda and Gamphani Lungu will miss both of Zambia's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Burundi after medical assessments found that each would need more than seven days to recover, ZamFoot reported on Tuesday 10 November. The team doctor, George Magwende, confirmed the withdrawals and said the players' clubs had been in contact with the Chipolopolo medical department. Coach George Lwandamina has called up Edward Chilufya for Daka, Derrick Bulaya for Banda and Prince Mumba for Lungu.

Daka hurt his right ankle in Hamburger SV's 3–1 Bundesliga win over Borussia Mönchengladbach on Friday 6 November, a game in which he played the full 90 minutes; Dr Magwende described it as a mild strain needing seven to ten days, ZamFoot reported. AfricaSoccer.com, reporting the club's confirmation, said he would stay in Hamburg for treatment during the international break and that the Hamburger Morgenpost expected him to be fit for the derby against Werder Bremen on 22 November. He had only recently returned from a thigh muscle tear.

Banda, of Al Swehly SC, has a left hamstring injury picked up on club duty that is expected to keep him out for at least two weeks, and Lungu, of Orlando Pirates, has a right ankle sprain with a recovery estimated at 14 to 21 days, ZamFoot reported. Kingstone Mutandwa, Ackim Mumba and Jackson Phiri were already unavailable for both fixtures.

On the same afternoon three Europe-based players landed at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport and connected to Ndola: the forward Chanka Zimba, recalled after his move to GD Vitória de Sernache in Portugal, the Cagliari midfielder Joseph Liteta and the Slovan Liberec defender David Hamansenya, ZamFoot reported in a second piece on Tuesday.

Zambia host Burundi at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Friday 13 November, with kick-off at 15:00, and play the return in Bujumbura on Tuesday 17 November. Zambia are second in Group I with three points from two matches, a point behind Algeria; Togo also have three and Burundi are bottom with one. Tickets are on sale through Computicket at Shoprite outlets at K50 for the north and south stands, K100 for the east stand, K250 for the west stand and K500 for VIP seats, ZamFoot reported. The finals will be co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania from 19 June to 17 July 2027.

body.title: Out and in
items: **Patson Daka** (Hamburger SV) — right ankle, 7–10 days; replaced by Edward Chilufya.
**Lameck Banda** (Al Swehly) — left hamstring, at least two weeks; replaced by Derrick Bulaya.
**Gamphani Lungu** (Orlando Pirates) — right ankle sprain, 14–21 days; replaced by Prince Mumba.
**Arrived Tuesday** — Chanka Zimba, Joseph Liteta, David Hamansenya.

stories.title: A K93 million KCM deal, 40% of the referees' arrears paid and Asanović's debt stretched to 2028: the Times of Zambia sets out FAZ's own account of 18 months of balance-sheet repair
stories.excerpt: Eighteen months after Keith Mweemba's executive took office, a Times of Zambia feature lays out what the association says it has done about money: a five-year sponsorship with Konkola Copper Mines, a committee tasked with raising US$30 million in two years, a referees' debt being cleared in instalments and separations from two former coaches without severance. The figures are FAZ's.

image.label: Football House ledger
image.caption: Sponsorship up, old debts being paid down: the association's version of its finances, two days after the President promised to help with a legacy debt.

body: The Football Association of Zambia has signed an extended five-year sponsorship with Konkola Copper Mines worth K93 million covering men's and women's competitions, on top of a K10.8 million KCM deal for the Copper Queens, the Times of Zambia reported on Tuesday 10 November in a feature on the association's finances since Keith Mweemba's executive committee took office in May 2025. The larger deal is expected to fund new cup competitions, including an FA Cup, the paper reported. The feature draws largely on Mr Mweemba's own account, and the figures in it are the association's rather than independently audited ones.

A Commercial and Marketing Advisory Committee has been given the job of mobilising about US$30 million over two years for football development, the Times reported. On the other side of the ledger, FAZ acknowledged in April 2026 a debt of about K7 million to lower-division referees; it says it has now cleared 40% of those arrears and expects to pay the remaining 60% before the new season starts.

body.text: We inherited outstanding financial obligations to referees
body.attribution: Keith Mweemba, FAZ president, as quoted by the Times of Zambia on Tuesday 10 November

body: Three former coaches' contracts account for much of the inherited liability. The obligations to the former Chipolopolo coach Avram Grant were resolved through a mutual separation with no severance payment, the Times reported, and about five months of salary arrears owed to the former Copper Queens coach Nora Häuptle were addressed, leading to what the paper called a mutually separated arrangement. The debt to Aljoša Asanović, another former Chipolopolo coach, has been restructured into a repayment plan that runs to 2028.

Mr Mweemba framed the aim as building an association that can generate sustainable revenue rather than relying on limited traditional funding, and said its success should not be measured by the number of announcements it makes, the Times reported. The feature appeared two days after President Hichilema, hosting the under-15 world champions at State House on Sunday 8 November, promised to invite the mining houses to a meeting to raise money for FAZ and to work with the association to dismantle a legacy debt that Open Zambia put at more than K140 million; he asked Mr Mweemba to put the association's concerns in writing and urged it to avoid new borrowing.

body.title: FAZ's figures, as reported by the Times of Zambia

**K10.8 million** — KCM deal for the Copper Queens.

stories.title: 'Easier to ship from Zambia to London than to Ghana': AfroQuality opens its first Lusaka store at Arcades to sell African brands across African borders
stories.excerpt: The pan-African retailer, which already has shops in Accra, Kigali, Nairobi and Dakar, has opened at Arcades Shopping Mall with a pitch to Zambian designers: a shelf in other African capitals. The Zambia Association of Fashion Designers' president Faith Kabende and FNB Zambia's Luyando Mumba spoke at the launch, the Times of Zambia reports.

image.label: Arcades, new tenant
image.caption: A store that says its job is to move African fashion between African countries, a trade its founders say is harder than exporting to Europe.

body: AfroQuality, a retailer that stocks fashion, accessories and other products from African brands, has opened its first store in Zambia at Arcades Shopping Mall in Lusaka, the Times of Zambia reported in a feature on Tuesday 10 November. The company already has stores in Accra, Kigali, Nairobi and Dakar, and its stated purpose is to give brands from one African country a route to customers in another.

Estella Malek, the group's Chief Curation, Logistics and Merchandising Officer, told the launch that the company had been set up to help African brands grow beyond their home markets, and described the difficulty of moving goods between African countries: it can be easier, she said, to ship a product from Zambia to London than to Ghana. She also said she wanted to change perceptions of African fashion, which she argued should not be confined to traditional fabrics and prints.

body.text: We call ourselves an engine, an engine that has built an ecosystem.
body.attribution: Estella Malek, AfroQuality Group, at the opening of the Arcades store, as quoted by the Times of Zambia on Tuesday 10 November

body: Faith Kabende, president of the Zambia Association of Fashion Designers and chief executive of Fay Designs, said the store would help Zambian designers reach buyers in other countries, and argued that young people who favour foreign fashion might come to value local culture through a shop of this kind. Fashion, she said, is not just clothing but identity and culture, the Times reported.

FNB Zambia's Business and Commercial Executive, Luyando Mumba, said the bank supports local businesses with market access and finance, pointed to its trade fairs as a way of opening new markets, and said that backing businesses like AfroQuality could benefit many people because small and medium-sized enterprises are the backbone of the economy.

The opening adds a cross-border retail channel to a Zambian fashion scene that has mostly reached foreign customers through fairs, social media and individual orders. Whether a Lusaka-made garment ends up on a shelf in Nairobi or Accra will depend on the curation and logistics the company says it has built; the Times feature gives no figures for the store's investment or the number of Zambian brands it has taken on.

sources.title: AfroQuality brings Africa's fashion to Zambia

stories.title: Kalambo, Chishimba and the Mwela rock art: the Culture minister visits Kasama and says the Northern Circuit needs roads, marketing and money to help reach five million visitors
stories.excerpt: Christopher Chibuye paid a courtesy call on Northern Province Minister Wedden Chileshe on Tuesday 10 November to see the state of the province's heritage sites. He called for investment in heritage infrastructure and better access roads, and said the Northern Circuit could contribute to the national target of five million tourist arrivals, Zambia Monitor reports.

image.label: The Northern Circuit
image.caption: Waterfalls, rock paintings and traditional ceremonies that the minister says are held back by the roads that lead to them.

body: The Minister of Culture and Arts, Christopher Chibuye, visited Kasama on Tuesday 10 November and said Northern Province's heritage sites needed investment in infrastructure, better roads and stronger marketing if they were to draw the visitors and investors the government wants, Zambia Monitor reported. He was shown the condition of the province's sites during a courtesy call on the Northern Province Minister, Wedden Chileshe, whose office arranged the visit to set out the challenges to their development.

The sites he named were Kalambo Falls, Chishimba Falls and the Mwela Rock Art Sites, along with the province's traditional ceremonies and other heritage assets. Mr Chibuye said the Northern Circuit could help the country reach its target of five million tourist arrivals, but that doing so would need informed interventions and stronger collaboration between government and other stakeholders to promote the attractions, improve infrastructure and make the area attractive to investors.

body.text: Culture defines our nation and must be preserved and promoted through the arts.
body.attribution: Christopher Chibuye, Minister of Culture and Arts, in Kasama on Tuesday 10 November, as quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: Mr Chileshe said the province was ready to work with the ministry and to help the sector contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda, and both ministers said tourism development would support jobs and local economic activity, Zambia Monitor reported.

No figures were given for what the heritage investment would cost, which sites would be prioritised, or when any road works might begin; the report records a statement of need rather than a programme. Nor did either minister say which agency, the Culture ministry, the National Heritage Conservation Commission or the road authorities, would be responsible for the works the minister called for.

Mr Chibuye's case, as Zambia Monitor reported it, was that the sites already exist and already draw ceremonies and visitors; what they lack is the road, the signage and the promotion that would turn them into a circuit. He asked for joint efforts by government and other stakeholders to promote the attractions, improve infrastructure and create an environment that investors would find attractive, and said that informed interventions and stronger collaboration would be critical to positioning the Northern Circuit for the five-million target.

analysis.title: A door opened is not a door walked through
analysis.body: Tuesday's ruling is narrower than the relief around it suggests. The High Court decided only that the 18 treason accused filed their bail application in a form the court can hear; it said nothing about whether they should be freed. That question, resting on Articles 13 and 28 and on how long someone may be held before trial, is still to be argued, and no date has been published. Two things make the next stage worth watching. First, the State has now lost a procedural objection in the treason case while raising a new, undisclosed one in the sedition case, so the pattern the defence complains of, delay by preliminary issue, will be tested again on Monday. Second, the court's reasoning on jurisdiction may settle how future constitutional bail petitions must be brought. The State's case, as argued so far, has been procedural: that the application was brought in the wrong form. The defence's is substantive: that 74 days without a bail hearing is itself the breach. The substantive hearing is where those two readings finally meet.

analysis.title: Counting teachers before hiring them is sound; moving 1,558 in a week is the hard part
analysis.body: Two ministers said the same thing from different ends of the system this week: the government does not know where its teachers are. Dr Musokotwane's examples, schools with an establishment of six carrying 25, others with five and only two present, describe a payroll that has drifted away from the classroom. Freezing recruitment until the count is done follows from that, and whatever the education budget is, it will stretch further if it pays people where they are needed. The Copperbelt order is where the policy meets its limits. Transfers are easy to announce and hard to execute: housing in rural districts, spouses' jobs, children's schooling and the Cabinet's own four-year rule all become live questions once 1,558 letters are issued, and the unions have not yet been heard. Watch whether the one-week assessment produces a list, whether the threatened dismissals are carried out, and whether other provinces follow. If the count is honest, it may also show that the shortage is smaller, or larger, than either minister expects.

analysis.title: Zambia's power problem has moved from the drawing board to the bank
analysis.body: The number that matters from Mr Kapala's visit to the regulator is not 10,000 but 16,000: there is more signed capacity in power purchase agreements than the 2031 target requires, and most of it is stuck at financial close. That changes what the government has to do. Signing more agreements will not help; persuading lenders that ZESCO and other buyers will pay, over the life of a plant, in a currency whose swings the IEA has flagged, will. The tools exist on paper, a procurement framework, published guidelines and a UK-backed liquidity mechanism, and the ERB chairman's complaint that financiers demand things the framework already covers suggests the gap is partly one of trust and paperwork rather than policy. The meeting with developers should show which projects are close, which are paper, and what guarantee the Treasury can afford, given the fiscal limits the World Bank described last year. The 945 MW added since 2024 shows it can be done; the next 5,000 MW depends on money that has not yet arrived.
